correctness.rationale: For a nontrivial finite abelian odd-order H, commutation of A with every {1,g} is equivalent to commutation with every identity-containing B by distribution over unions. Taking complements gives C∩Cg=C∩gC. In additive notation on H, the rotation tests give S∩(S-k)=S∩(S+k); testing at a∈S with k=b-a shows closure under x↦2a-x. Such reflections compose to translations by twice each difference; multiplication by two is invertible on every subgroup of H, yielding S=a+K for K generated by the differences, and then K=S-S. Conversely a coset passes every rotation test. The reflection tests are automatic for S empty; otherwise the rotation component at r∈R says 2r stabilizes S, equivalent to r∈K, and the reflection component at any t∈S says membership of x and -x in R agrees for every x. These conditions suffice as well. There are [H:K] cosets, and (|K|-1)/2 inverse pairs outside the identity, giving exactly the subgroup sum plus the 2^(|H|-1) unrestricted branch. The subgroup counts for the cyclic and elementary abelian groups of order nine give 287 and 305. /workspace/branches/independent_dihedral.py tested direct products against every B for H=C3, and direct two-point products for C5,C7,C9,C3×C3, with counts 9,25,79,287,305 and element-wise agreement with the classification; the general proof uses the above subgroup argument, not finite extrapolation.

value.rationale: The center is a natural isomorphism invariant for this canonical construction. The theorem identifies all of its elements, explains why reduction permits new central subsets, and reduces its size to data about the subgroup lattice. The order-nine examples distinguish two same-order kernels at the level of reduced power monoids; they illustrate the structural result rather than serving as the main evidence. The odd-order coset rigidity is a nonmechanical step beyond elementary two-point testing.
